Pele Yoetz 307:3: And there is no trouble in the world as great as the trouble of the soul, and it is fitting for a person to precede trouble with prayer and pray and pour out his soul before the Name, that He be with him in his trouble, and that He help him struggle with the evil inclination and be saved from pride, anger, harsh temper, robbery, deceit, and forbidden speech, and other such prohibitions that a person is liable to transgress, and that they help him serve the Name with a complete service, and to say prayers and blessings with intention, and to fear and love the Name and cling to Him and the like, to fulfill every good thing. Over all this let him pour out his soul before the Name — perhaps there is hope, and the righteous shall be delivered from trouble (and regarding this too I intend, without a vow, with the help of Heaven, to lift my hand [i.e., compose something]). And prayer bears fruit and shall remind him to stand on guard.
Pele Yoetz 307:4: “And a man's gift makes room for him” (Proverbs 18:16), for a man gives his soul's ransom to the Name. Great is charity, for it annuls the decree and gives life to those who perform it, as it is written (ibid. 10:2), “And charity delivers from death.” And it is written (ibid. 21:21), “Whoever pursues charity and kindness finds life.” And when he gives the charity, let him make his trouble known to the many, and the recipients must pray for the giver, that he be saved from his trouble, and through this relief and salvation shall stand firm.
Pele Yoetz 308:1: Tziyur (Visualization) — Visualization is a thing that is exceedingly beneficial, for it was written in the name of the Ari, of blessed memory, that in order to fulfill “I have set the Lord always before me” (Psalms 16:8), one should constantly visualize before his eyes as though the Name “Havayah” were written before him in Assyrian script, vocalized to be read thus: YHVH, and this is exceedingly beneficial for fear of Heaven. And likewise they said in the Talmud (Sanhedrin 22a) that one who prays should see himself as though the Divine Presence were before him. And regarding every transgression that comes into his hand, and every good thing his inclination entices him not to do, let him visualize as though standing before the Name, who is a King exalted and lofty, awesome and fearsome (as is indeed true), and He says to him in a great, thunderous voice, “And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might” (Deuteronomy 6:5), and as though he sits between the Garden of Eden and Gehinnom — if he does good, he shall enter the Garden of Eden and delight in abundance for his soul, and if a bad deed, he shall immediately fall into Gehinnom. And let him imagine terrifying, alarming images that would frighten him and cause him anguish of soul.
Pele Yoetz 308:2: And the kabbalists wrote that one should always visualize before his face the image of his teacher's face, which is exceedingly beneficial for the attainment of wisdom. And likewise they wrote that one should visualize the image of his father before his face when lying down to sleep, which is beneficial for being saved from nocturnal emission. And those engaged in the wisdom of Kabbalah have seen how much the power of visualization, imagination, and thought accomplishes, and prophecy and the rectification of the worlds depend almost entirely on this. Go and learn from the four who entered the Orchard (Chagigah 14b), that it was all through deepening the thought of visualization. And the kabbalists wrote: whatever place a person considers and attaches his thought to, there is the position of his soul — happy is he who chooses and draws near to dwell in glory within the sanctuary; a person sanctifies himself from below, and they sanctify him from above.
Pele Yoetz 309:1: Tzipui (Anticipation) — It is known that one of the questions asked at the Day of Judgment is, “Did you anticipate salvation?” (Shabbat 31a), and this is a matter entrusted to the heart, for it does not suffice to say with the mouth that he anticipates salvation, but rather he must anticipate salvation with a whole heart and complete faith. For just as every day a person draws closer to death, so every single day the redemption draws closer, and if it tarries, we shall wait for it, for it shall surely come without any doubt. And it is not only for the redemption that one must sit and anticipate, but for every trouble that may come upon a person, one must anticipate the Lord's salvation in the blink of an eye.
Pele Yoetz 309:2: And it was already written in the name of the Ari, of blessed memory, that every day when one says, “For Your salvation I have hoped all the day” (Genesis 49:18), he should intend that he anticipates salvation for every trouble he finds himself in, and this is very effective. And let him intend, when he says “For Your salvation,” that he is not concerned for himself but only for the grief of Heaven, for “in all their affliction He was afflicted,” and he anticipates that the Holy One, blessed be He, will act for the honor of His own Name — hence specifically “Your salvation.” And since he anticipates salvation, let him be careful to guard against everything that delays the salvation, and to do every good thing, for our entire aim and desire is for the salvation of the Name and the redemption of the Divine Presence.
Pele Yoetz 309:3: Behold, therefore, a man cannot say: “Is the redemption delayed because of me, or is it in my power to bring it closer even if I were a perfectly righteous man? Behold, there are opposed to me several thousands of Israel, a people walking in darkness, worse than I, and had I known that this trouble was because of me and that the redemption was delayed on my account, I would have put myself to death over Torah and Divine service.” But this is vanity, since it is the redemption of the Divine Presence that we seek, and it is explained in the holy Zohar that every commandment Israel performs lightens the wings of the Divine Presence and she flies upward, and for every transgression each individual Israelite commits, the wings of the Divine Presence are weighed down and she descends below. For this let a man tremble and be seized with great dread, and let him watch and observe and do all that is in his power to do in order to raise the Divine Presence from the dust. And how much more so, since when the time to be gracious to her arrives, for the appointed time known to the God of knowledge, the Lord, has come, even through one Israelite who performs complete repentance, the redemption can be brought closer. And as our sages, of blessed memory, said in the Midrash on the verse “Return, O Israel” (Hosea 14:2) — that this is why it is stated in the singular.
Pele Yoetz 309:4: And after God has made all this known to you, understand well the statement of our sages, of blessed memory (Yerushalmi Yoma 1:1), who said: “Whoever does not have the Holy Temple built in his days, it is as though it were destroyed in his days,” and he is destined to give an account for not having withheld his hand from transgressions and not having done all that was in his power to bring the Name's salvation closer, in such a way that there be no delay on his account, and that some portion of the redemption of the Divine Presence come through him. And all this is the fruit of anticipating salvation. And one who does all that is incumbent upon him to do receives his reward in full, and the Holy One, blessed be He, accounts it to him as though He had redeemed him and his children, and as though the Holy Temple had been built in his days.
Pele Yoetz 310:1: Tzibbur (Congregation) — They said in the holy Zohar (part 1, p. 234) that the prayer of an individual does not ascend before the holy King except with great strength, for the Holy One, blessed be He, examines it and looks into his sins, whereas the prayer of the many ascends entirely before the Holy One, blessed be He, without His looking into their sins. And the reason for the greatness of the merit of praying with a congregation is: first, because of the response of the craftsmen [i.e., the congregational responses], such as “Yehei shmei rabba,” “Barechu,” and “Kedushah,” which are of great value. Second, that a few performing a commandment is not comparable to many performing it, for it is far more effective. And third, that an individual's prayer, if it lacks intention, or if he is a person with transgressions and the like, is not accepted, but when joined with the many, it is accepted. And now there are many common people who easily neglect praying with a congregation for some minor reason, and eventually it comes to be treated as permitted, and they neglect it even without any reason at all, and go from bad to worse, praying a hurried and truncated prayer, and not at its proper time, and sometimes not praying at all.
Pele Yoetz 310:2: And Mahari already wrote in the book Kikar LaAden, and these are his words: “Trembling has seized me, how the reins have been loosened to pray individually, and even beyond the time of the Shema, for our sages, of blessed memory, said (Zohar part 3, p. 186) that he is liable to excommunication, and in the Midrash Konen they said that he is liable to excommunication for neglecting Kaddish and Kedushah.” And our sages, of blessed memory, in the first chapter of Berachot (8a), and in the holy Zohar (Bereishit, part 1, p. 234), elaborated greatly on the merit of praying with a congregation, and the matter is an a fortiori argument to persist in this. And we have already written on this above under the entry “Minchah,” and the preachers have already expounded this and that and the other, and cried out like cranes, but would that their hearts were inclined to heed the words of the wise, that they might inherit good in this world and delight in abundance for their souls in the World to Come.
Pele Yoetz 310:3: The obligation to honor the congregation, and the severity of the prohibition against troubling the congregation, is explained thoroughly, like a well-fitted garment, in the book Shalmei Tzibbur — see there. And according to its severity, one must be exceedingly careful. Every Torah scholar in his community is obligated, if he sees that [the prayer leader] prolongs his prayer or is late in coming, to warn the synagogue attendant not to wait for him, for it is better for a person to pray individually in his home than to trouble the congregation. And if the congregation forgoes its honor and wishes to wait, he should not agree to it nor accept it.
Pele Yoetz 310:4: And according to what is written there, that the prohibition against troubling the congregation is not specific to the synagogue, but applies to any gathering of ten, a person should learn from this that when he is invited to some assembly, such as a feast or a meeting, the diligent hasten to go among the first of those invited, and should not trouble the many to wait for him. And who is honored? He who honors his fellow creatures (Avot 4:1), and how much more so the congregation, for the Holy One, blessed be He, cherished their honor above His own, as is known from several prohibitions that were permitted for the sake of the congregation's honor and because of the trouble to the congregation (Shabbat 81). And whoever is careful and concerned about the trouble to the congregation and the honor of the congregation shall find favor and good understanding in the eyes of God and man.
Pele Yoetz 311:1: The letter Kuf: Kedushah (Holiness) — A person who sanctifies himself from below, they sanctify him from above; one who sanctifies himself a little, they sanctify him greatly; one who sanctifies himself in this world, they sanctify him for the World to Come — so said our sages, of blessed memory (Yoma 39a). And behold, a person's sanctification depends on guarding against every sin, in thought, speech, and deed. And especially, wherever you find a fence against forbidden relations, you find holiness. And the fence against forbidden relations is that he shut his eyes from seeing evil and remove from his heart strange thoughts and evil musings, and since he sanctifies his eyes and his heart, which are the two agents of transgression, he shall automatically merit to arrange holiness and his entire body shall be sanctified. And this is the plain meaning of the verse that is written (Numbers 15:39), “And you shall not go about after your heart and after your eyes,” etc., “so that you remember,” etc., “and you shall be holy to your God.” And this is why it is written (Proverbs 23:26), “Give Me your heart, my son, and let your eyes observe My ways.”
Pele Yoetz 311:2: And the kabbalists already wrote that with every limb through which a person commits a transgression, he draws a spirit of impurity upon it, upon the limbs of his soul, spirit, and higher soul. Correspondingly, the limb with which he performs a commandment draws upon it a flow of holiness — except for the sin of wasted seed, which defiles all his limbs from head to toe. And this is the reason “one commandment leads to another commandment, and one transgression leads to another transgression” (Avot 4:2), for in holiness his limbs are the Sanctuary of the Name, as our sages, of blessed memory, said regarding the verse (Exodus 25:8), “And let them make Me a sanctuary, and I shall dwell among them” — it is not said “within it” [the sanctuary], but “among them” [the people]. And it is possible that the Divine Presence is with him even while a transgression comes through his hand, for although he himself does not see it, his fortune [i.e., his soul] sees it (Megillah 3a), and the soul shall be seen [i.e., held back] from sinning, as I have written in the name of our teacher, Rabbi Shmuel Primo. But when he sins and defiles his limbs, the Divine Presence departs from him, as it is written (Deuteronomy 23:15), “And He shall not see among you any unseemly thing and turn away from you,” and immediately the Sitra Achra rests upon him, and he goes from evil to evil, may the Merciful One save us, and he does not feel it, for he is like a dead man, and dead flesh does not feel the scalpel — so he does not feel and is not concerned, even if he hears a thousand rebukers, his uncircumcised heart will not be subdued, he neither ails nor senses — and all according to the impurity and the darkness upon his soul, spirit, and higher soul, which is a curtain separating between him and his Father in Heaven.
Pele Yoetz 311:3: Behold, therefore, the man who is a Jew, while his eyes are still open, before the sun grows dark and before the days of evil come, should feel bitter about this — that he does not feel it at first — and say, “Woe is me, for I have been ruined; behold, I have perished, I have been lost, Heaven forbid,” and let him gather all his strength and might to remove the spirit of impurity, little by little driving it away from himself, and acquire a flow of holiness by guarding against every evil thing and doing all the good that is in his power, day by day going and growing, going and returning, until he is purified and a steadfast spirit is renewed within him, like another man and a new creature, for one who comes to purify himself is assisted [from Heaven]. And it is written in the books that it is good to say before performing any commandment:
Pele Yoetz 311:4: “Behold, I am summoning such-and-such limb to fulfill such-and-such commandment, for the sake of the unification of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Divine Presence,” for through this the Sitra Achra turns away from there and holiness rests.
Pele Yoetz 311:5: And if through all the commandments holiness rests upon a person, how much more so through the observance of Shabbat, which is the first of the holy convocations. And especially at the time of reciting the Kedushah, let him intend with great intention and much humility. And let him precede, on the sixth day, thoughts of repentance and purification through immersion in a mikveh of purity — perhaps he shall merit that an additional soul, spirit, and higher soul rest upon him, and a flow of holy holiness of Shabbat, and from there it shall extend to all the weekdays, to help and benefit the service of the blessed Name. And likewise, in the congregational response of Kedushah, when saying “the whole earth is full of His glory,” let him intend to draw upon himself a flow of holiness from the holiness above, and let him intend that he is ready to give his life for the sanctification of the Name, to fulfill what is written (Leviticus 22:32), “And I shall be sanctified among the children of Israel,” whenever the opportunity comes to him, for through this his soul, spirit, and higher soul are sanctified.
Pele Yoetz 311:6: And the great principle in acquiring holiness for himself and drawing a holy soul for his offspring is the sanctification of thought, that he persist in it according to his ability — even in passing, coming and going, let him remember the Rock of his holiness and fulfill the commandment to fear and love the honored and awesome Name and cling to Him, and this is a hard service indeed, for a person has no control over his spirit, and thought is beneficial yet fleeting; but it is a person's duty to pursue it and do all that is in his power to do, like a man of war rousing himself from his sleep, until a spirit from on high is poured upon him and he finds the means of his redemption, and he shall live and shall be holy.
Pele Yoetz 312:1: Kimah (Rising) — Rising before an elderly person and before a Torah scholar is one of the 613 commandments, and many treat it with disdain and lose much good over trivial matters, for they said (Bamidbar Rabbah 15:17) that whoever fulfills this commandment merits fear of Heaven (and if he has this intention when standing before an elder — to correspond to the “beard of the Long-Suffering One” [a Kabbalistic term] — and when standing before a Torah scholar — to correspond to the “beard of the Short-Suffering One” — he also merits to grow wise in Torah, so wrote the Ari, of blessed memory), as it is written (Leviticus 19:32), “You shall rise before gray hair,” etc., “and you shall fear your God” — is there such good reward in the world as this? And likewise before his father and mother and before his teacher he is obligated to rise at least twice a day, and some say he is obligated to rise even a hundred times, only they said (Kiddushin 33a) that whoever waives it, let him waive it, so as not to trouble them. And this applies specifically when he sees that commandments are not dear to them, or that they do not rise at all, as in an orphaned generation like this one, for then he transgresses “before the blind you shall not place a stumbling block”; but if commandments are dear to them, it is better to pass before them so that they perform the commandment and give satisfaction to our Creator and receive good reward. And I have already proven this elsewhere from the language of the Yerushalmi.
Pele Yoetz 312:2: And the obligation to rise before gray hair, according to the holy Zohar, applies from the time one reaches sixty years of age. And a Torah scholar who studies halachot and knows how to argue reasoning well is obligated to be honored by rising his full height, not as is done now, where they rise only slightly, seen and not seen, for they did not say this suffices except for Torah scholars and elders. And they already said in the Talmud (Makkot 22b), “How foolish are those who rise before a Torah scroll but do not rise before a Torah scholar.” And regarding such a thing we have learned (Avot 4:2), “Be as careful with a minor commandment as with a major one, for you do not know the reward given for commandments.”
Pele Yoetz 312:3: And just as a person is careful and diligent to fulfill the commandment of the shofar blast, the lulav, the sukkah, tefillin, and the like, so must he be careful to fulfill all the commandments of the Torah and even more so, for they punish more severely for a minor commandment, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Menachot 43a): “Greater is the punishment for white [tzitzit strings] than the punishment for blue.” To what is this comparable? To two men to whom the king said: to one he said, “Bring me a seal of clay,” and to the other he said, “Bring me a seal of gold,” etc. And one who guards a commandment shall receive great reward, and how much more so this commandment [of rising], for its reward is good since it leads to the commandment of fearing the Name.
Pele Yoetz 313:1: Keriah (Reading) — How many trustworthy readings there are, such as the reading of the order of the sacrifices, Psalms, the Ma'amadot, and many others — books full of them; but the intention of the heart is what matters, and a little with intention is better than much without intention. And let the one choosing choose according to his knowledge and according to the free time available to him, taking advice from a Torah scholar as to which reading is more important to recite before the Omnipresent, blessed be He. And how good and pleasant it is for him to carry in his bosom a small book of Psalms or of ethical teaching on Shabbat in his shop, keeping it with him and reading in it whenever he is free, and let him not worry about the mockery of the complacent or the gentiles. There are already gentiles who do this with their own heretical books, so why should we be lesser? And perhaps someone in whose heart fear of the Name has touched shall learn from him, and it turns out that he merits and causes merit — and greater is Torah, for it is fitting that it protect and bring blessing, and it is considered for him as though he were engaged in halachic study, and as though he read the entire day, and his witnesses vindicate him.
Pele Yoetz 314:1: Kinah (Jealousy) — Jealousy is an exceedingly evil trait, as the Tanna said (Avot 4:21), “Jealousy, lust, and honor remove a person from the world.” And behold, the inclination of a person's heart is evil, and desires to be unique in his generation in wisdom, deeds, wealth, and honor, and through this he grieves when there is another like him or greater and better than him, and he becomes jealous of him and seeks his harm and speaks of his disgrace. And great is the hatred that comes from jealousy — it is a consuming fire with no remedy. And whoever has this evil trait has pains all his days, eats the bread of sorrow, has no beloved friends, increases disputes, rejoices at calamity, and desires his fellow's stumbling, that his fellows stumble in a matter of halachah, that they fall short in the service of the blessed Name, that they have diminished stature and limited comprehension, and many other such evils and offshoots that are dragged along from jealousy. And who could describe the greatness of its evil? Whoever desires life should flee from it and be a mighty man who conquers his inclination through deepening pure thoughts, believing with complete faith that no person touches what is prepared for his fellow, and even if he were the only one in the world, he would not gain more than what is decreed for him. And even if merchants like him multiply into thousands and myriads, he shall lack nothing of what is fixed for him. And let him be content with what is the Creator's will, the Rock whose work is perfect, and to each one, that which is good for him, he does.
Pele Yoetz 314:2: And all of Israel are one body like one man, and it is fitting to rejoice at one's fellow's good fortune and to grieve at his trouble as though it were his own, and especially bearing in mind that even when the wicked are in distress, the Divine Presence grieves — what does the tongue say, etc. Correspondingly, when Israel is at ease, the Lord shall rejoice in His works. And furthermore, when a person is in pressure and grief, he cannot serve his Creator, and the pressure causes him to transgress against his own understanding and against his Maker's will, and this is grief for Heaven; whereas when he is at ease and calm, he increases doing good and gives satisfaction to his Maker. And when the wicked are in the world, there is wrath in the world, and “when straw is taken out, [the wicked] is beaten like Rava” [i.e., the wicked also suffer along with judgment upon the wicked] (Bava Kamma 92a). And when the righteous are in the world, abundance and great blessing increase, and with the increase of goodness, its eaters increase.
Pele Yoetz 314:3: And one who loves his father and mother with true love, a love of the soul, thinks: let good come to my father and satisfaction before him regardless — what does it matter to me whether through me or through others, since I do not serve in order to receive a reward, but only wish for my father and mother's satisfaction. So should a person say: whether through me or through them, let the One on High be praised. And if it were possible that of all the commandments I perform, I would benefit not myself but only others, who would delight in abundant peace (in the manner of “the whole world is sustained for the sake of my son Chanina”), and that all the suffering I endure and the self-mortification I undergo would benefit not myself at all, but only atone for the sins of the generation — I would not be concerned at all. And how much more so if they told me: if you wish to benefit yourself, only one sin will be atoned for you, but if you agree to benefit another, two sins will be atoned for him — I would certainly choose to benefit another rather than myself, since I am not concerned for myself, but only to give satisfaction to my Creator. Such and such things let the living take to heart, and strengthen himself with pure thoughts to remove jealousy from his heart and evil from his flesh, and let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice in the good fortune of Israel, whether in their bodies, their money, or their souls, and let him grieve over their loss as though it were his own.
Pele Yoetz 314:4: But there is a good jealousy, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Bava Batra 21a): “The jealousy of scribes increases wisdom.” And let him desire and strive to ascend in the levels of wisdom and the service of the blessed Name like the holy ones who are in the land, and a person is obligated to say, “When will my deeds reach the deeds of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob?” (Tanna DeVei Eliyahu Rabbah 25). And if he sees that his fellow succeeds in his deeds, let this be his jealousy, that he say, “Certainly all depends on a person's deeds; the fruit of his actions shall he eat.” And let his heart be jealous in the fear of the Name, in the manner of what is written (Genesis 30:1), “And Rachel was jealous of her sister,” and our sages, of blessed memory, explained (Bereishit Rabbah 71:6) that she was jealous of her good deeds, for she said, “Had she not been better than I, she would not have merited to be built up [with children].” And through this he shall improve his deeds to give satisfaction to his Maker, for this is the whole of man.
Pele Yoetz 314:5: And there is yet another kind of jealousy that is exceedingly good: to be jealous with the jealousy of the Lord of Hosts, to break the fangs of the wicked and raise up the banner of the Torah. And the merit of Pinchas is known, a zealot son of a zealot, who was zealous with the jealousy of the Lord of Hosts, and the Name called him “peace.” And through this the tribe of Levi was praised: “Who said of his father and mother, I have not seen him” (Deuteronomy 33:9). And they already said in the Talmud (Berachot 20a): “Why did miracles happen for the earlier generations, and why do miracles not happen for the later generations — is it because of their Torah study?” etc. And they answered: the earlier ones gave their lives for the sanctification of the Name, as in the incident where Rabbi Adda saw a certain woman wearing shatnez [forbidden mixed fabric], and he arose and tore it off her, etc. And if the merit of one who gives himself over to death rather than transgress those transgressions for which they said, “Let him be killed rather than transgress,” is great, how much greater still is the merit of one who gives his life to be jealous with the jealousy of the Lord of Hosts, to break the fangs of the wicked, save the oppressed, and protest with all firmness against those who commit transgressions, and the like. And according to the greatness of its value and importance, so is it difficult to find, for through our sins flattery has grown strong and love of the blessed Creator has diminished, for this depends on the greatness of one's love. To what is this comparable? To one who sees another striking his father and mother with a cruel blow and cursing and reviling them — he cannot restrain himself from giving his life for them to save them, and like a man of war he shall rouse a battle and not turn back for anyone's sake — how much more so for the honor of our Father in Heaven, for “anger toward his father is a foolish son, and bitterness to his mother” [a paraphrase]. And certainly one who is zealous for the honor of the Omnipresent and does all that is in his power to do, no evil shall befall him, and those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing, for the Name is their help and their shield.
Pele Yoetz 315:1: Kelalah (Curse) — A curse is a grievous evil to the one who curses, and the one who curses shall be divided as spoil — they shall both eat their portions [i.e., both suffer]. For if it is a baseless curse, without guilt, it shall return to its place. And it is written in Sefer Chasidim (section 76) that sometimes even if the curses are not deserved, they return upon the one who curses. For thus we find that all the curses David cursed Joab were fulfilled through David's own offspring (Sanhedrin 48b). And if the curses are fulfilled, behold, he is destined to give an account, for he causes his fellow to be punished and evil to come upon him through him. And sometimes curses are fulfilled even from the mouth of a lightweight and common person, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Megillah 15a): “Never let the curse of a common person be light in your eyes, for behold, Abimelech cursed Sarah and it was fulfilled in her offspring.” And it all depends on the hour and the moment — blessing and curse can both be fulfilled; there is a time of favor and a moment of His anger. Behold, therefore, it is good for a man — “one who has a good eye shall be blessed” (Proverbs 22:9) — to turn a curse into a blessing. When he hears the voice of those who curse, let him respond, “It shall not be so, but rather blessed shall it be” — perhaps there is hope that no evil shall befall.
Pele Yoetz 315:2: And behold, this evil trait is mostly found among women, who are irritable, loud-voiced, and quick to curse, and their mouths fill with harsh curses toward their children, and they know very well that this is not good, and they do not wish their children any harm, not even to their little finger, but because of their anger, they cannot restrain their words. It turns out that one who curses shows a bad sign, that he has become very angry indeed. And it is known that one who becomes angry is as one who worships idolatry (Nachmanides on Deot [Maimonides]; Rambam's commentary on Avot 2:10), and one transgression drags another transgression (Avot 4:2; Tanchuma, Teitzei 1).
Pele Yoetz 315:3: And behold, if the curse upon their children is fulfilled, woe to them, for they are slaughterers of children and are destined to give an account; and if it is not fulfilled, certainly their merits are deducted — either from the one who cursed or from the one cursed — for the attribute of justice prosecutes and demands that the curse be fulfilled, except that merit intervenes, and it turns out that he constantly consumes his own merits. And there are several who hear from preachers this and that and the other, and their hearts ache, but they do not abandon their evil habit, for they say, “We cannot restrain ourselves and cannot abandon our custom, for such is the habit of the tongue,” and it puts on cursing like its garment. But this is a false answer, for whatever a person desires, he can do if he wishes — little by little he can abandon this evil way through vows and penalties, that he change and substitute it. And if he wishes to soothe his irritation, let him say in his anger, in the manner of some virtuous women who say, “May no evil come upon you; may evil come upon the enemies; may the name and memory of Amalek be blotted out,” and the like.
Pele Yoetz 315:4: And truly, the fact that people are not habituated against this is an exceedingly great wonder — how do they not tremble with great dread to let a curse issue from their mouths against their children, or against any one of the children of Israel, and wish them harm? Ears should tingle at hearing this. And it would be better for them to strike them with a heavy blow, for if he strikes him with a rod he shall not die, but through a curse he could die, may the Merciful One save us. Whoever desires life, guard your tongue from evil and your lips from curses.
Pele Yoetz 315:5: And it is known that one of the 365 negative commandments is not to curse any Israelite, and if he is not in his presence, he transgresses (Leviticus 19:14), “You shall not curse the deaf.” And since our sages, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 55a; see also Kiddushin 61b), that the guest who blesses the host is himself blessed, because it is written (Genesis 12:3), “And I will bless those who bless you,” we learn from this that one who curses an Israelite shall be cursed, as it is written there, “And he who curses you I will curse.” Behold, therefore, let a man be careful and guard himself, and warn his wife and all who are under his authority, that no curse be heard from their mouths, but only blessings above all, and through this the Lord shall command the blessing to be with you (Deuteronomy 28:8).
Pele Yoetz 315:6: And it is likewise fitting for a person to be careful and guard against causing a curse upon himself even from the mouth of a gentile, and all the more so and how much more so that they should not cause their father and mother anger to the point of cursing them, for woe to the children who bring their father and mother to such a great sin, for this is a far greater evil than if they had struck them, and they shall certainly be punished, for if the evil of one who causes others to sin is great, how much more so one who causes his father and mother to sin through the sin of anger, which is exceedingly severe and causes a curse upon himself — evil shall come upon them, Heaven forbid. But a wise son gladdens his father, for his entire aim is to do his father and mother's will instantly, obediently, without transgressing, and upon him shall come the blessing of good from his father and mother, and he shall carry a blessing from the Lord, and He shall repay him that he have worthy sons who do his bidding and his will as his own will.
Pele Yoetz 316:1: Kabbalah (Tradition) — Tradition is a great principle in the Torah, and almost the majority of the Torah in our hands is by way of tradition, for Moses received the Torah from Sinai, and every generation received ruling from ruling. And even now that books have multiplied, there are several matters that a person cannot ascertain the truth and clarity of except through a practical ruling that he saw or heard from the mouth of a great man. And therefore they said (Berachot 7b), “Greater is [attending on sages and] serving them than studying [under them],” for with his own eyes he shall see and with his own ears he shall hear which is the straight way, since even if a man lived a thousand years he could not reach the end of the books and know all the laws in their entirety, as is fitting to do. But one who attends upon Torah scholars and rolls in the dust of their feet shall add knowledge day by day — what shall the son do so as not to sin? And sometimes, when he is eighty or ninety years old, he shall hear something new that he never knew before.
Pele Yoetz 316:2: However, regarding the matter of tradition, great care is needed lest one err in his own imagination, for the flame has fallen even upon the cedars. And the sages of the Talmud said (Eruvin 53a), “We are like a finger in a wax seal compared to forgetfulness” [i.e., our memory is inferior]. And from this were born several disputes in the Talmud, where one says thus and another says thus, and how much more so we, orphans of orphans, for we have grown very poor and forgetfulness is common. Therefore it is not fitting for a person to testify and say something in the name of its speaker unless the matter is as clear to him as his own sister [i.e., absolutely certain], in any case where the speaker is not present before him to ask him. And even if it seems to him that the matter is as clear as his own sister, he should still be concerned lest he err.
Pele Yoetz 316:3: And he should not act upon relying on his own tradition, or tell others to be lenient in any prohibition, even a minor one, without first searching the books to see if they agree with his tradition, as Rava said in the Talmud (Bava Batra 130b): “If a legal ruling of mine emerges before you and you see in it something wondrous [i.e., questionable], do not tear it up, and do not act according to it.” (And I too, poor and lowly, command with all firmness that no one should act to be lenient based on a tradition in my name, even if the one saying it says the matter is as clear to him as his own sister — do not heed him, until you search to know the law thoroughly from the mouths of books and from the mouths of the holy authors who are in the land. For several times things are testified before me in my name that I never said and that never entered my mind, or it is possible that I too erred in things I said or did, and I retract them, and I am not fit to be relied upon for leniency. And out of worry and grief I command this commandment with all firmness, and let it not be transgressed, and to those who hear it, it shall be pleasant, and upon them shall come the blessing of good.) But he should hold to the beneficial half: that tradition is beneficial for stringency and conducting oneself piously, for whoever is stringent, the blessing of good shall come upon him.
Pele Yoetz 317:1: Kevi'ut (Fixed Times) — Fixing times for Torah is one of the things a person is asked about at the Day of Judgment: “Did you fix times for Torah?” (Shabbat 31a). And now the book Chok LeYisrael has become renowned throughout all the dispersions of Israel. And it is one of those things where a little sustains much and is very valuable, for in a little time one studies all kinds of study, having a hand in everything, arranged according to the secret teachings from the circle of the Ari, of blessed memory, and he builds his chambers in heaven and learns from it wisdom, ethics, and laws. And how good and pleasant is the custom in some cities, where those who fear the Name and esteem His Name gather together to study the order of Chok LeYisrael, and the wise among them reads aloud and explains to them the halachah, and sometimes the holy Zohar, and the order of Yosef LeChok, in such a way that every person, even the most common, can merit to study this study after the Scripture reading, and there is added also the merit of studying this publicly and reciting the Kaddishes, and this study is so important.
Pele Yoetz 317:2: And it grieves me for many of our brothers, the children of Israel, who are chasing after vanity, and before the prayer has even finished they flee to their work and their labor, losing much good. For if it were in my power, I would take hold of all our brothers, the children of Israel, by the collars of their garments, and bind them with chains of iron and ropes of the cords of love of the blessed Name, that they stand a short time to study, and even one who has no book should listen as though reading, and they shall gain much good. And just as in the commerce and trade of this world it is sometimes found that a person buys an item cheaply and gains immense wealth from it, so it is with this matter: with a little study he gains much more than if he engaged for many hours in the laws of leprosy and tents [difficult, less practically urgent areas of study].
Pele Yoetz 317:3: And great is the fixing of times for Torah, for we have established (Ketubot 15a) that anything fixed is considered as half and half [i.e., as if it occupies half the time], and it turns out that the Name accounts it to him as though he studied Torah half the day, and the One abundant in kindness inclines toward kindness, and rewards those who establish fixed times with great reward, as though they studied the entire day and the entire night, never silent. And who has seen and heard such things and would not desire to merit to study this and gain much good? May the Name put it in their hearts to draw near to holiness and give satisfaction to our Creator — “day to day utters speech” (Psalms 19:3). And night to night let him fix for himself some study as his means allow, and through this he fulfills his obligation and fulfills the verse that is written (Joshua 1:8), “And you shall meditate on it day and night.” But these measures were stated only for one whose circumstances are exceedingly pressing, who is very occupied with his work and labor from morning until evening for his sustenance and livelihood — even so, this does not exempt him from fixing times for Torah, the minimum being like the morning, afternoon, and evening prayers.
Pele Yoetz 317:4: And the merit of fixed times is that this time be fixed for his study, and he not exchange or substitute it, even if he has much business and thinks he could gain much during that time — let him not worry and not turn back for anyone's sake from abandoning his fixed time, and the Name shall repay him, for those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing (Psalms 34:11). But if he has free time, it does not exempt him from the great and awesome Day of Judgment, even if he studied Torah much that day, as it is written (Job 7:19), “You do not let me alone even to swallow my spittle,” and our sages, of blessed memory, explained that even for the brief time it takes to swallow saliva, one is destined to give an account of how it was spent. Woe to us from the Day of Judgment and from the depth of judgment. And it is known, the statement of Rabbi Yishmael to his nephew, after he had studied the entire Torah and wished to learn Greek wisdom, and he said to him, “Go find an hour that is neither day nor night, and study Greek wisdom then” (Menachot 99b). And it is stated in the Midrash on the verse (Psalms 119:126), “It is time to act for the Lord, they have violated Your Torah” — whoever fixes times for Torah violates the covenant (Yalkut Shimoni, Psalms, remez 878). And the commentators explained (Rashi there) that this means: whoever fixes times and relies on this to spend the rest of his free time in idle sitting and idle talk, turning himself over to idleness.
